notes: The only carded record is CORE, a position/argument (a safety-case sketch), graded ARGUMENT_ONLY. The sketch relies on a forthcoming protocol (prover-estimator debate) that is not specified in this paper.

method.description: Safety-case sketching: a hypothetical structured argument, relying in part on future research, that a developer could make for a debate-trained AI R&D agent, organised around four key claims.

passages.text:
This paper sets out what debate can be used to achieve, what gaps remain, and what research is needed
to solve them. The paper uses the technique of safety case sketching (Hilton et al., 2025): outlining an
argument a developer could make that a given AI system is safe in a given context. The details in the sketch
are hypothetical, often relying on future research. Nonetheless, the sketch helps contextualise how different
pieces of evidence fit together and identify the most crucial pieces of missing evidence.

We imagine starting with a pre-trained model (e.g. an LLM trained on next-token prediction) and then
fine-tuning it via a debate which satisfies the above requirements. We wrote it with a particular protocol
in mind, called prover-estimator debate (forthcoming), but the argument structure should be applicable to
other protocols as well. In prover-estimator debate, a “prover” (Alice) produces subclaims arguing for a
conclusion to a given query, while an “estimator” (Bob) assigns probabilities to the subclaims.

Two copies of the model debate each
other via a carefully specified protocol
and adjudicated by simulated human
judges, until they reach an equilibrium
in which the models provide honest
answers most of the time.

stated_hypotheses: The deployment context is low-stakes, so online training can limit the effect of distribution shift; the sketch argues this assuming sufficient security in the environment implementation.
Exploration guarantees rule out exploration hacking during training.
The debate protocol avoids obfuscated arguments; the protocol the sketch relies on needs a stability assumption.
The human input being simulated has bounded systematic error with respect to reality, and its simulation has bounded systematic error with respect to that input.
The model does not deliberately underperform during training.

passages.text:
The core claim in the sketch is that debate training can upper bound the proportion of model outputs that are
1
misaligned, as long as the model does not deliberately underperform during training. This upper bound can
be maintained during deployment if a system is trained continuously. So, in low-stakes settings, where
a small number of mistakes are acceptable such that you can use online training (Christiano,
2
2021), debate training might be sufficient - especially if the error bound is tight.
The sketch focuses on a slightly superhuman system in a limited internal deployment context designed for
automated AI research (including alignment research). The sketch argues that this is a low-stakes context,
assuming sufficient security in the environment implementation. The paper also contains ideas about pushing
low-stakes solutions through to high-stakes contexts (see “Extending the safety case to high-stakes contexts”).

setting.systems: A hypothetical slightly superhuman LLM agent; two copies of the model debate each other (prover-estimator debate as the example protocol)
setting.task_data: Hypothetical internal deployment for automated AI research inside an AI company

limits.notes: The sketch covers only low-stakes contexts; the authors say the argument is not strong with current techniques and that the sketch's details are hypothetical.

strength.reason: The passages present a hypothetical argument that relies on future research; no proof or experiment for the four claims is given in them.
